analysis.one_liner: Requires credit score creators to publish their scoring methods and report debt settlements.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it was introduced in September 2014 with no cosponsors and died in the House Financial Services Committee when the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change the Fair Credit Reporting Act so that any company that builds a credit score — the three-digit number that decides whether you can rent an apartment, get a car loan, or get a credit card — has to make its scoring tool or system available to the public, including on its website. It would also strike current law that says credit bureaus do not have to explain your score to you or handle your disputes about it. Finally, if you settle a debt with a creditor for less than you owe, the creditor would have to tell the credit bureaus within 30 days so your credit report shows the settlement.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers whose lives are shaped by credit scores. Today, the formulas behind those scores are trade secrets; this bill would let anyone see exactly how a score is calculated. People who pay less than the full balance on a debt through a settlement would get that settlement recorded on their credit report promptly instead of being stuck with stale, incorrect information.

how_it_helps.text: Any person or company that develops a tool or system for deriving a credit score must make it available to the public, including on its website, so consumers can see how their score is calculated.
The bill removes existing FCRA provisions that say the law cannot be read to require credit bureaus to disclose score information to consumers or to explain and handle disputes about scores.
Creditors who furnish debt information would have to notify credit bureaus of any settlement agreement with a consumer within 30 days.

analysis.who_pays: Credit scoring companies and consumer reporting agencies, which would have to disclose methods they currently keep as trade secrets, and creditors or debt collectors who would face a new 30-day reporting duty for settlements.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit scoring firms and credit bureaus

drawbacks.text: Credit scoring models are proprietary products; forcing companies to make their tools or systems fully public could give credit-repair outfits a roadmap for gaming scores and could blunt the incentive to develop better models.

The bill was introduced late in a two-year session with zero cosponsors and was never acted on, so its provisions received no committee scrutiny, and a disclosure mandate this broad raises practical questions about what 'make such tool or system available' actually requires.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the upside is real: score transparency and accurate reporting of debt settlements address two persistent complaints about the credit reporting system. The cost falls on scoring companies and bureaus rather than consumers, though the full-public-disclosure approach is blunt compared with narrower 'adverse action' explanation rules that already exist. The bill was too vaguely drafted and too lightly considered to know how it would have worked in practice.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in September 2014, near the end of the two-year session, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Kerry Bentivolio, a Republican from Michigan, introduced the bill on September 16, 2014, less than four months before the 113th Congress ended.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day, which is where any action would have had to start.
No other member of the House cosponsored the bill.
The House took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit scoring companies and credit bureaus are better off: they never had to open up their scoring methods or take on a new settlement-reporting duty. Consumers lost a chance at transparency into the numbers that govern their access to credit.

for.name: Rep. Kerry Bentivolio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 16, 2014 and offered no further action before leaving office; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in September 2014 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by one Republican and had no cosponsors from either party, so no meaningful partisan pattern ever emerged.

industries.note: Companies that develop credit scores would have to make their scoring tools or systems public, ending the trade-secret basis of their business. Their interest in keeping formulas secret runs directly against consumers' interest in knowing how they are judged.

The bill removes legal language shielding bureaus from any obligation to disclose score information, explain scores, or handle score disputes, but it also creates a new information flow (settlement notices from creditors) they would have to process. The net effect is more disclosure burden and less discretion over what they tell consumers.

Anyone furnishing debt information would face a 30-day deadline to report settlement agreements with consumers. Honest creditors lose little; debt buyers and collectors who profit when settled debts linger on reports as unpaid lose accuracy they currently are not forced to correct.
